SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION AND APPROVAL OF THE RELOCATION IMPACT REPORT
(“RIR”) FOR THE BELL MOBILE HOME PARK LOCATED AT 4874 E GAGE AVENUE

RECOMMENDATION:

IT IS RECOMMENDED THAT THE CITY COUNCIL:

  1.  Discuss and approve the RIR for the Bell Mobile Home Park located at 4874 E
  Gage Avenue
  2.  Read by title only, waive further reading and adopt Resolution No. 2026-63 titled:

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF BELL
  APPROVING THE RELOCATION IMPACT REPORT FOR THE
  BELL MOBILE HOME PARK

BACKGROUND

The Bell Mobile Home and RV Park located at 4874 Gage Avenue in the City of Bell, California
(“Park”) was privately developed in the 1940’s. The 151-space Bell Mobile Home Park (8.56
acres) (“Park”) was privately developed in 1946. Currently, residences occupy only 115 of the 151
Park spaces. The Bell Community Housing Authority (“BCHA”) acquired the Park in 1995 to
improve the BCHA’s supply of affordable housing, and in 2005 refinanced the Park by issuing a
$20.8 million bond issue.

BCHA makes the payments on the bonds and covers the operational costs for the mobile home
parks, including maintenance, utilities, insurance and personnel costs. BCHA utilizes the rents
collected from the residents as a portion of the revenue to cover operating costs.

BCHA bond obligations are required to make annual payments of approximately $1.3 million per
year, and to have a $1.3 million bond coverage contingency, and the city is required to backstop
any deficiencies.

For several years BCHA has been suffering a structural deficit, that has been increasing annually;
and it is projected that BCHA’s operating deficits will negatively impact on the City’s General Fund
by subsidizing the BCHA fund.

  1
 BCHA rent levels in the Bell Mobile Home Park range from $492.83 to $800 per month and haven’t
been increased by BCHA in 15 years. A survey of nearby mobile home parks indicated that rents
averaged $1,265 a month, demonstrating that BCHA rents are substantially below market.

BCHA spends annually $$4,101,023.80 on operations, including maintenance, utilities,
personnel, and insurance with estimated increasing costs on future maintenance.

DISCUSSION

In 1978 the State enacted the Mobile Home Residency Law (“MRL”) which provides a
comprehensive regulatory scheme governing the use, conversion and closure of mobile home
parks. Pursuant to this law, BCHA hired Overland, Pacific & Cutler, Inc. (“OPC”) to prepare a
Relocation Impact Report Replacement and Relocation Plan (“RIR”) which could be enacted to
protect residents in case of a relocation process, and a state certified appraiser to do a market
analysis of the supply, demand, and marketability of privately owned mobile homes in the region.
BCHA and OPC held numerous community meetings in both English and Spanish to prepare the
RIR, including on September 22, 2025, October 13, 2025, October 15, 2025, November 6, 2025,
and November 17, 2025. Bell Mobile Home Park residents were also provided with an opportunity
to schedule personal meetings with OPC relocation personnel to provide information about their
households, dwellings, relocation needs and the potential impact a park closure would have on
their households. Relocation agents attended community meetings and remained afterwards to
schedule many of the residents for personal interviews. OPC also provided phone availability after
hours and on weekends, and specifically from February 2, 2026, through February 24, 2026.

On August 5, 2026, BCHA facilitated hand-delivery of the RIR to all residents and non-resident
owners and BCHA gave notice of the date, time and place for the public hearing to be held by the
City Council on October 14, 2026. Additionally, the RIR was posted on the City’s website for public
review.

The City Council’s action on the RIR does not have the potential for resulting in either a direct
physical change in the environment, or a reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
environment. The City Council’s consideration of the RIR relates only to the determination of the
measures required to be taken to mitigate the adverse impacts on Park residents who will be
displaced should the Park be sold or closed.

There is no redevelopment of the property which is currently proposed in connection with the RIR.
Additionally, approval of the RIR does not constitute “approval” of any “project” for purposes of
CEQA, because the RIR is not a project, and because approval of the RIR does not commit the
City to sell or close the park immediately.

Upon review of the RIR and consideration of the written and oral evidence received at the hearing;
the City Council further finds as follows:

The RIR provides reasonable measures which meet and exceed the requirements of state law to
mitigate the adverse impact of the park closure on the ability of the park residents to be displaced
to find alternative housing.

Some of the provisions that the RIR provides for applicants to take the following measures to
mitigate the adverse impacts on the park residents to be displaced by the park closure:

  In situations where it is feasible to relocate a mobile home to a comparable park within a
  reasonable distance and the mobile home owner (with the assistance of the relocation

  2
 specialist provided by applicant) has located a new location that will accept the coach, RIR
mitigation shall be provided as follows:

  a.  Reimbursement for the actual cost to relocate the mobile home,
  including without limitation, to disassemble, transport, reassemble,
  and level the mobile home and all legal accessory structures
  (awnings, skirting, porches, storage structures, etc.) to another
  mobile home park within 50 miles of the Park;
  b.  Full replacement cost of any items damaged during the move,
  substantiated by receipts or appraisals from a licensed appraiser;
  c.  Transportation of the home by a licensed, bonded, and insured
  mover, who will disconnect and reconnect all utilities and obtain all
  required permits;
  d.  Compensation to install improvements, if required at the new park,
  such as new steel supporting piers, skirting, and/or landscaping;
  e.  Payment of temporary lodging and food expenses or daily living
  expenses, if the mobile home relocation results in the homeowner
  being displaced over one or more days, limited to current housing
  and per diem rates for Los Angeles County at the time of
  displacement and a reasonable number of days as approved by the
  owner;
  f.  Payment of moving costs associated with moving all personal
  property, allowance to be determined based on the most current
  federal fixed move schedule for the State of California and the size
  of the mobile home and/or based on professional mover bids,
  including packing and unpacking, if selected by the resident;
  g.  A 3 ½ years (42-month) space rent differential payment, if the
  monthly space rental rate in the replacement mobile home park (not
  to exceed the space rental rate of comparable space rent as
  determined by the owner) is greater than the current space rental
  rate at the Park.
  h.  Payment for necessary modifications to the mobile home to
  accommodate a handicapped or disabled person to comply with
  decent safe and sanitary requirements;
  i.  Services of a relocation specialist to assist owners through aspects
  of the relocation to include, but not be limited to, an explanation of
  options and relocation assistance program details, identifying
  replacement units, coordinating moving arrangements and
  payment of benefits, and additional services as described on pages
  13-17 of the RIR; and
  j.  Payment of a one-time required park entrance fee.

In situations where it is not feasible to relocate the mobile home to a comparable park
within a reasonable distance, and the mobile homeowner procures/acquires a
replacement dwelling or rental unit, RIR mitigation shall be provided as follows to every
resident who selects this option:

  k.  Payment to the mobile homeowner for the appraised in-place
  market value of the dwelling and all associated fixed property as
  determined by the qualified appraiser, pursuant to a Purchase
  Agreement;
  l.  Reimbursement of eligible non-recurring closing costs associated
  with selling the Park unit to the new owner;

  3
   m.  Payment of moving costs associated with moving all personal
  property, allowance to be determined based on the most current
  federal fixed move schedule for the state of California and the size
  of the displacement dwelling and/or professional mover bids,
  including packing and unpacking, if selected by the resident;
  n.  For owners that elect to purchase replacement housing (25 CCR
  §§ 6102, 6112(c)(5)(A)-(B)), a Price Differential Payment equal to
  the difference between the purchase price of a comparable
  replacement dwelling or the actual cost of the replacement dwelling,
  whichever is less, and the amount paid by the new owner for the
  Park unit (paragraph 1 above);
  o.  For owner-occupants that elect to purchase replacement housing
  (25 CCR §§ 6102, 6112(c)(5)(A)-(B)), a Mortgage Interest
  Differential Payment will be provided if there is an existing mortgage
  or loan on the Park unit and the owner-occupant cannot secure the
  same interest rate or a lesser interest rate on financing used to
  purchase the replacement dwelling;
  p.  For owner-occupants that elect to purchase replacement housing
  (25 CCR §§ 6102, 6112(c)(5)(A)-(B)), non-recurring closing costs
  related to the purchase of a replacement dwelling will be
  reimbursed to the owner-occupant;
  q.  For owner-occupants who elect to rent rather than purchase
  replacement housing (25 CCR §§ 6104, 6112(c)(5)(C)), a rent
  differential payment (in accordance with 25 CCR § 6104). In
  calculating this payment, where an owner-occupant elects to rent a
  replacement manufactured home or mobile home and site, the
  average monthly rental shall equal the economic rent for the
  manufactured home or mobile home plus the actual rent for the site;
  r.  Services of a relocation specialist to assist owners through aspects
  of the relocation to include, but not be limited to, explaining options
  and relocation assistance program details, identifying replacement
  units, coordinating moving arrangements and payment of benefits,
  and additional services as described on pages 13-17 of the RIR;
  and
  s.  Upon receiving title to the dwelling pursuant to a purchase
  agreement, the owner will pay for the cost of disposing of the
  dwelling.

In addition to these payments and support for owners of mobile home units, non-owner
tenant occupants will be eligible under the RIR for the following assistance:

  t.  Payment of moving costs associated with moving all personal
  property, allowance to be determined based on the most current
  federal fixed move schedule for the state of California and the size
  of the displacement dwelling and/or professional mover bids,
  including packing and unpacking, if selected by the resident;
  u.  Each tenant household will receive a rent differential payment if the
  monthly rental rate of the replacement dwelling (not to exceed the
  rental rate of a comparable dwelling as determined by the Owner)
  is greater than the current rental rate at the Park. The rent
  differential payment will be calculated based on 42 months of
  assistance. This payment may also be converted to Down Payment

  4
   Assistance to be applied toward the purchase of a comparable
  replacement dwelling; and
  v.  Services of a relocation specialist to assist owners through aspects
  of the relocation to include, but not be limited to, explaining options
  and relocation assistance program details, identifying replacement
  units, coordinating moving arrangements and payment of benefits,
  and additional services as described on pages 13-17.

Upon approval of the RIR, BCHA will complete a revised housing survey completed and collect
household documentation to determine any last resort housing benefits to the extent required by
applicable laws (including 25 ccr §6139). To the extent the cost of the replacement housing
exceeds the dollar thresholds in relocation guidelines, additional payments will be authorized
above these thresholds as necessary to provide any required “last resort housing” benefits in
existing housing resources available in the area.

Residents will work with the BCHA-provided relocation specialist identified in the RIR to identify
the appropriate relocation housing for them, and if the costs of such housing exceed the resident’s
base replacement housing assistance eligibility dictated by the above-referenced dollar
thresholds, additional funds will be authorized to provide the “last resort housing” benefits
consistent with title 25, section 6139 of the California code of regulations.

The RIR addresses the availability of adequate replacement housing in mobile home parks; and
addresses relocation costs, including the costs of moving a mobile home or purchasing an
available mobile home in another park or other available housing. These relocation costs are
further addressed in the RIR with mitigation measures that include payment of all moving costs
related to personal property, payment of first and last month’s rent, and payment of security
deposit and relocation assistance.

Prior to any potential displacement of any resident, the resident shall receive at least six (6)
months’ written notice pursuant to the civil code.

Staff believe that the RIR, attached hereto as Attachment A, is adequate and sufficient to address
the availability of adequate replacement housing in mobile home parks and relocation costs
including the costs of moving a mobile home and purchasing an available mobile home in another
park or other available housing.

Staff position is that if it retains ownership, it is unlikely it would have the financial resources to
manage the property long-term and it will negatively impact the City’s General Fund. Also, future
financial projections project that BCHA could potentially violate its bond covenants and require a
subsidy from the City to meet the deficit obligations.

Conclusion
For the reasons stated above, staff recommend that the City Council approve the RIR.

   RESOLUTION NO. 2026-63
  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF BELL
  APPROVING THE RELOCATION IMPACT REPORT FOR THE BELL
  MOBILE HOME PARK

  WHEREAS, the Bell Mobile Home and RV Park located at 4874 Gage Avenue in the
City of Bell, California (“Park”) was privately developed in the 1940’s. The Bell Community
Housing Authority (“BCHA”) acquired the Park in 1995 to improve the BCHA’s supply of
affordable housing; and

  WHEREAS, for years BCHA has suffered structural deficits, due in part to the
operational costs and maintenance of the Park, which has required BCHA to utilize reserve
funds and at times, borrow funds from the City of Bell’s General Fund to cover the BCHA’s
funding deficit; and

  WHEREAS, as a result of BCHA’s inability to continue providing for the long-term
financial support of the Park and the ongoing fiscal instability it is creating for BCHA, including
its maintenance and operational costs, capital investment needs, and liability exposure, BCHA
commenced with the process for the closure and/or conversion of the Park; and

  WHEREAS, in connection therewith, BCHA, along with its consultants, Overland, Pacific
& Cutler (“OPC”), held various community meetings for Park residents to discuss the potential
Park closure and process, which all Park residents were invited to attend (via written letters);
such meetings occurred on September 22, 2025 at City Hall, October 13, 2025 and October 15,
2025 at the Park, and again on November 6, 2025, and November 17, 2025 at City Hall. The
meetings were conducted in English and Spanish, and Park residents were provided an
opportunity to schedule personal meetings with OPC relocation personnel to provide information
about their households, dwellings, relocation needs and the potential impact a Park closure
would have on their households; and

  WHEREAS, California Government Code Sections 65863.7 and 66427.4 and Civil Code
Section 798.56, govern the requirements for an impact report and the mitigation measures as a
condition of conversion of an existing mobile home park to another use or closure of a mobile
home park or cessation of use of land as a mobile home park; and

  WHEREAS, BCHA has submitted to the City Council, for its approval, a Relocation
Impact Report Replacement and Relocation Plan (“RIR”) a copy of which is attached hereto as
Exhibit “A” and incorporated herein by reference, to determine the relocation impacts and
relocation impact mitigation measures related to its proposed closure of the Park; and

  WHEREAS, on August 5, 2026, as required by law, BCHA sent notice of, and a copy of,
the RIR to all Bell Mobile Home and RV Park owners and residents and gave notice by certified
mail to the residents, and any nonresident owners of mobile homes in the Park of the date, time
and place for hearing of the application of approval for the RIR by the Bell City Council on
October 14, 2026. The RIR was also posted on the City’s website for public review on August
5, 2026; and

  WHEREAS, on September 30, 2026, BCHA and OPC held an informational meeting at
the Bell Community Center regarding the RIR for all mobile home residents to attend, wherein

  1
 OPC and BCHA staff presented the RIR and discussed the associated process and answer
resident questions; and

  WHEREAS, California’s Mobile Home Residency Laws (“MRL” or “Relocation Laws”)
(codified in Cal. Govt. Code Sections 65863.7-65863.8, 720 et seq.; Cal. Civil Code Section 798
et seq., and in the Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Guidelines adopted by
the Department of Housing and Community Development as Title 25, Cal. Code of Regulations
Section 6000, et seq.) provides a comprehensive regulatory scheme governing the use,
conversion and closure of mobile home parks and ensure the protection of residents in case of
a relocation process. The MRL also requires a public hearing on the RIR, prior to any potential
Park closure; and

  WHEREAS, on August 5, 2026, the RIR was mailed to all residents and non-resident
owners and BCHA gave notice of the date, time and place for the public hearing to be held by
the City Council on the RIR (i.e., October 14, 2026). Additionally, on August 5, 2026, BCHA also
hand-delivered Spanish versions of the cover letter and notice for the public hearing, and follow-
up notices were delivered to all Park residents on October 9, 2026; and

  WHEREAS, on October 14, 2026, the City Council held a duly noticed public hearing
regarding the consideration of approval for the RIR for the Park as required by law and received
comments and testimony both orally and in writing and considered all evidence and testimony,
including the measures required to mitigate the adverse impacts on displaced residents in the
event of a closure of the Park.

NOW THEREFORE, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF BELL DOES HEREBY FIND,
DETERMINE, AND RESOLVE AS FOLLOWS:

  SECTION 1. The foregoing recitals are true and correct and are incorporated herein as
findings of fact.

  SECTION 2. The City Council finds any consideration of or action upon the RIR is not
subject to review under the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) because neither the
RIR nor the City Council’s or BCHA’s action thereon constitutes a “project” within the meaning
of CEQA. (Pub. Res. Code §21065; 14 CCR §15378). The City Council’s action on the RIR
does not have the potential for resulting in either a direct physical change in the environment, or
a reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment. The City Council’s
consideration of the RIR relates only to the determination of the measures required to be taken
to mitigate the adverse impacts on Park residents who will be displaced should the Park be
closed. No redevelopment of the property is currently proposed in connection with the RIR.
Additionally, approval of the RIR does not constitute “approval” of any “project” for purposes of
CEQA, because the RIR is not a project, and because approval of the RIR does not commit the
City to a definite course of action or foreclose options or alternatives in regard to any project
intended to be carried out by any person, and because it does not constitute a commitment to
issue or the issuance of a discretionary contract, grant, subsidy, loan, or other form of financial
assistance, lease, permit, license, certificate, or other entitlement for use of a project (14 CCR
§15352).

  SECTION 3. Upon review of the RIR and consideration of the written and oral evidence
received at the hearing, the City Council finds and determines as follows:

  2
 A.  Pursuant to Government Code Section 65863.8, BCHA satisfactorily verified and
  demonstrated to the City that all Park residents and mobile homeowners have
  been notified of the proposed Park closure and the City Council’s hearing on the
  RIR in the manner prescribed by law. The RIR was also posted to the BCHA’s
  website.
B.  BCHA and OPC held numerous community meetings in both English and
  Spanish in connection with the preparation of the RIR, including on September
  22, 2025, October 13, 2025, October 15, 2025, November 6, 2025, and
  November 17, 2025. Park residents were also provided with an opportunity to
  schedule personal meetings with OPC relocation personnel to provide
  information about their households, dwellings, relocation needs and the potential
  impact a Park closure would have on their households. OPC relocation agents
  attended the community meetings and remained afterwards to schedule many of
  the residents for personal interviews. OPC also provided phone availability for
  residents after hours and on weekends, and specifically from February 2, 2026,
  through February 24, 2026.
C.  The RIR provides reasonable measures which meet and exceed the
  requirements of state law to mitigate the adverse impact of the Park closure on
  the ability of the Park residents to find alternative housing. The RIR provides for
  the following measures to mitigate the potential for such adverse impacts:
  1.  In situations where it is feasible to relocate a mobile home to a
  comparable park within a reasonable distance RIR mitigation and
  assistance shall be provided as follows (all as further detailed in the RIR):
  (a)  Reimbursement for the actual cost to relocate the mobile home,
  including without limitation, to disassemble, transport, reassemble,
  and level the mobile home and all legal accessory structures
  (awnings, skirting, porches, storage structures, etc.) to another
  mobile home park within 50 miles of the Park;
  (b)  Full replacement cost of any items damaged during the move,
  substantiated by receipts or appraisals from a licensed appraiser;
  (c)  Transportation of the home by a licensed, bonded, and insured
  mover, who will disconnect and reconnect all utilities and obtain all
  required permits;
  (d)  Compensation to install improvements, if required at the new park,

Introduction

The Bell Mobile Home & RV Park is a 151-space residential mobile home park (“Park”)
situated on real property located in Bell, CA. The property is currently owned and operated
by the Bell Community Housing Authority (“BCHA” or “Owner”). The Owner of the Park
wishes to cease operating the Park and intends to follow the regulatory process to seek
approval of the Park closure. Future development plans for the site have not been
approved and are not known at this time.

As part of the Park closure approval process, the Owner is required to prepare this
Relocation Impact Report with a Replacement and Relocation Plan (collectively the
“Report”) in accordance with the State of California Government Code and Mobile Home
Residency Law (Civil Code Section 798 et seq.) (“MRL”) which provides a comprehensive
statewide regulatory scheme governing the use and closure of mobile home parks (Civil
Code sections 798 et seq. and Government Code sections 65863.7-65863.8.). In
addition, California State AB 2782 amended Civil Code Section 798.56 and Government
Code Section 65863.7 to impose additional requirements to be discussed later in this
Report.

Relocation assistance to Park residents will be provided per the requirements of
Government Code 7260 et seq. and the Relocation Assistance and Real Property
Acquisition Guidelines adopted by the Department of Housing and Community
Development as in Title 25, California Code of Regulations Section 6000, et seq. (“State
Relocation Regulations”). The aforementioned MRL, Civil Code, and Government Code
provisions (including as amended by AB 2782) and State Relocation Regulations are
collectively referred to herein as “the Laws”.

The purpose of the Report is to report on the impact of the proposed Park closure on
existing Park residents and to address measures to be taken to mitigate adverse effects
of the proposed closure upon the residents of the Park, who would be displaced by the
closure. In anticipation of the need to prepare for closure of the Park, Overland, Pacific &
Cutler, LLC (a GFT, Inc. company) or OPC, has been contracted to prepare this Report
as required by the Laws.

This Report explains the protections afforded the residents of the Park. Among the
requirements of Government Code Section 65863.7 are to “report on the impact of the
conversion, closure, or cessation of use of the mobile home park, include a replacement

The Report is to include a replacement and relocation plan that adequately mitigates the
impact upon the ability of the displaced residents of the mobile home park to be converted
or closed to find adequate housing in a mobile home park; or, if a displaced resident
cannot obtain adequate housing in another mobile home park, for payment to the
displaced resident of the in-place market value of the displaced resident's mobile home.
The relevant statutory law for the closure of a mobile home park and specific requirements
for mitigation are California Government Code Section 65863.7, Civil Code Section
798.56(g), and as amended by State AB 2782, which indicates that prior to closure City
Council will review the Report and any additional relevant documentation, and may

The most immediate impact of a possible Park closure is the effect on the mobile home

All residents face the issue of the disposition of their mobile home and relocation to a
replacement dwelling. Physical relocation of the existing dwelling to another mobile home

vicinity. Finding available alternative space, particularly for older mobile homes, will be a

The number one concern of the Park residents is the potential financial impact resulting
from the loss of affordable pad rent in the event they must relocate to a more expensive
park or conventional market-rate rental housing, and/or the financial inability to purchase
or rent a desirable replacement dwelling in a safe and nearby area, if their existing
dwelling cannot be relocated. Many of the residents are elderly, disabled and/or on fixed
incomes, and there is a high percentage of Extremely Low and Very Low Income
households within the Park.

Some Park residents require ramps and rails and are concerned with their ability to
relocate to an accessible unit. Resident owners with disability and mobility challenges,
including the need for wheelchair access, creates the need for these owners to secure
replacement housing capable of accommodating the physical disabilities.

Many interviewed residents expressed the need to remain close to their medical facilities,
family, schools and employment. And finally, some of the interviewed households have
indicated they have invested significant amounts of money to remodel or improve their
Park dwellings and are concerned with the appraisal process and recouping their
investments.

D. Replacement Housing Payments – Owner-Occupants
To be eligible to receive replacement housing assistance benefits, the displaced owner-
occupant household must have actually owned and occupied such dwelling for not less
than 180 days prior to the initiation of negotiations for its acquisition (or otherwise as
provided in 25 CCR §6102), and must purchase or rent and occupy a decent, safe, and
sanitary replacement dwelling within one year from the date on which final payment was
received from BCHA of all costs of the acquired dwelling, or the date on which the
household moves from the acquired dwelling, whichever is later. A displaced owner-
occupant may be eligible for a Replacement Housing Payment not to exceed $22,500,
except in the case of Last Resort Housing (discussed in Section G below). The
Replacement Housing Payment is comprised of three potential payment types (25 CCR
§§6102, 6112):

Price Differential Payment
 A payment will be provided to cover the increased cost the displaced owner-occupant
may have to pay when purchasing a replacement dwelling. The payment will be based
on the difference between: (i) the cost of a comparable replacement dwelling (i.e., a
replacement mobilehome, plus the amount necessary to lease, rent or make a
downpayment on a replacement site, or if a mobilehome is not available, a conventional
replacement dwelling, as provided in 25 CCR §6112(c)(5)(A)-(B)) (as determined by the
BCHA) or, if less, the cost of the replacement dwelling the Park resident actually
purchases; and (ii) the price paid by BCHA for the Park unit (Section B above).

Mortgage Interest Differential Payment
If a Park resident (owner-occupant) currently has a mortgage or loan on the dwelling, a
payment will be offered to the displaced Park owner-occupant to address the loss of
favorable financing, if the displacee’s existing mortgage/loan interest rate is less than the
interest rate that can be secured on a loan related to the replacement dwelling.

There is ample available housing in the City of Bell and other nearby communities for the
residents of the Park. While no two communities are alike, the residents undoubtedly have
quality, well-maintained mobile home park communities and other comparable
alternatives available for their consideration as housing options.

If the objective of Park residents were to continue owning a mobile home, resident owners
could be assisted to purchase a replacement mobile home using the payment for the
appraised in-place market value of their home and a potential Price Differential Payment.
We have concluded that it will be challenging to move existing mobile homes to another
park in the immediate vicinity, although if there are spaces available in other parks willing
to accept older units, the Park resident would be provided all moving and related costs
as outlined on page 13.

If purchasing a replacement mobile home is considered an option, buyers will find an
adequate inventory of for-sale mobile homes in good parks throughout Los Angeles
County and surrounding counties. Park residents may also consider purchasing a single-
family residence or townhome as alternative options for replacement housing.

A.  RELOCATION PAYMENT TAX CONSEQUENCES

In general, relocation payments are not considered income for the purpose of Division 2
of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, which has been redesignated as the Internal
Revenue Code of 1986 (Title 26, U. S. Code), or for the purpose of determining the
eligibility or the extent of eligibility of any person for assistance under the Social Security
Act (42 U. S. Code 301 et seq.) or the Personal Income Tax Law, Part 10 (commencing
with Section 17001) of the Revenue and Taxation Code, or the Bank and Corporation Tax
Law, Part II (commencing with Section 23001) of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation
Code. The above statement on tax consequences is not intended as tax advice by BCHA
or OPC. (Please note, any payment a dwelling owner receives for an existing Park
dwelling is not considered a relocation payment and may be subject to taxes). Residents
and dwelling owners are responsible for consulting with their own tax advisors concerning
the tax consequences of relocation or other payments.

B.  RELOCATION NOTICES

There are three principal notices that will be issued prior to any obligation to relocate:

  1)  Information Statement
  2)  Notice of Relocation Eligibility
  3)  180-Day Vacate Notice/Notice of Termination of Space Tenancy

Each notice, which the Owner is required to provide to a Park occupant, shall be
personally delivered or sent by certified or registered first-class mail, return receipt
requested and documented in the case file. Each notice will be written in plain,
understandable language. Each notice will indicate the name and telephone number of a
person who may be contacted for answers to questions or other needed help.

The Informational Statement (Exhibit J) is intended to provide potential relocatees with
a general written description of the Owner’s relocation program and basic information
concerning benefits, conditions of eligibility, noticing requirements and appeal rights.

A Notice of Relocation Eligibility (NOE) will be distributed to each Park household. The
NOE to the residential relocatee contains a determination of eligibility for relocation

D.  GRIEVANCE PROCEDURES

A person who is dissatisfied with a determination as to eligibility for benefits, a payment

practices may file a Relocation Assistance Appeal Form or any other written form of
appeal with the Owner and have the right of administrative review. The Owner’s appeal
policies will follow the standards described in Sections 6150 et seq. of the State
Relocation Regulations.

Requests for administrative review and informal hearings will be directed to the City
Manager, Michael L. Antwine II, who may be reached at mantwine@cityofbell.org or
323.588.6211. All requests for review will receive written responses from the Owner within
three weeks of their receipt. If an informal appeal is denied, appellants will be entitled to
file a written request for a formal hearing before an impartial and independent hearing
officer.

The appellant does not have to exhaust administrative remedies first; the
appeal/grievance can either go directly to the City, directly to HCD or directly to the Court.

  condition; is the result of harassment or retaliatory action; or, is the
  result of discontinuation, or a substantial interruption of services;
  (b)  Performance of a dangerous, and/or illegal act in the unit;

  notification within a reasonable time following Notice;

  (e)  Refusal to accept one of a reasonable number of offers of
  replacement dwellings; and/or,

  (f)  A requirement under State, or local law or emergency circumstances
  that cannot be prevented by reasonable efforts on the part of the
  Owner.

  3.  The Owner reserves all rights and remedies available to it pursuant to
  California Civil Code Section 798.56.

1. GENERAL INFORMATION

The dwelling in which you now live is in a mobile home park that is subject to closure by the
Displacing Agency using state and/or local funds. If and when the closure proceeds, and it is
necessary for you to move from your dwelling, you may be eligible for certain benefits. You will
be notified in a timely manner as to the date by which you must move. Please read this
information, as it will be helpful to you in determining your eligibility and the amount of the
relocation benefits you may receive under the state law. You will need to provide adequate and
timely information to determine your relocation benefits. The information is voluntary, but if you
don’t provide it, you may not receive the benefits or it may take longer to pay you. We suggest
you save this informational statement for reference.

The Displacing Agency has retained the professional firm of Overland, Pacific & Cutler, LLC
(OPC) to provide relocation assistance to you. The firm is available to explain the program and
benefits. Their address and telephone number is listed on the cover.

PLEASE DO NOT MOVE PREMATURELY. THIS IS NOT A NOTICE TO VACATE YOUR
DWELLING. However, if you desire to move sooner than required, you must contact your agent
at OPC, so you will not jeopardize any benefits. This is a general informational brochure only,
and is not intended to give a detailed description of either the law or regulations pertaining to
the Displacing Agency’s relocation assistance program.

Please continue to pay your rent to your current landlord, otherwise you may be
evicted and jeopardize the relocation benefits to which you may be entitled to receive.

2. ASSISTANCE IN LOCATING A REPLACEMENT DWELLING

replacement dwelling by providing referrals to appropriate and available housing units. You are
encouraged to actively seek such housing yourself.

When a suitable replacement dwelling unit has been found, your relocation agent will carry out
an inspection and advise you as to whether the dwelling unit meets decent, safe and sanitary
housing requirements. A decent, safe and sanitary housing unit provides adequate space for its
occupants, proper weatherproofing and sound heating, electrical and plumbing systems. Your
new dwelling must pass inspection before relocation assistance payments can be authorized.

The Displacing Agency will pay for all actual, reasonable, and necessary costs associated with
moving a Park resident’s dwelling to another available location within 50 miles of the Park, if the
home can be relocated. For mobile homes, assuming the mobile home could be moved and there
was an available location, these costs may include, but are not limited to, the cost to disassemble
the existing mobile home and all appurtenances in the Park, to transport the dwelling, and to
reassemble the mobile home and all appurtenances in another mobile home park or location.
Costs to move a travel trailer or RV to a location within 50 miles of the Park will also be paid for
by the Displacing Agency, but would not require assembly.

The Displacing Agency will also provide a 42-month space rent differential payment, if the monthly
space rental rate in the replacement mobile home park (not to exceed the space rental rate of
comparable space rent as determined by the Owner) is greater than the current space rental rate
at the Park.

 5. ACQUISITION PAYMENT - HOMEOWNERS

In the event a mobilehome, trailer, or RV cannot be moved to another mobilehome or RV park,
the Displacing Agency will agree to purchase the unit from the dwelling owner based on the
appraised in-place market value. Acquisition Payments will be made to the dwelling owners who
sign a Purchase and Sale Agreement and a Tenancy Termination Agreement and provide clear
title to their units. The Displacing Agency will provide an appraisal of the current dwelling at no
cost to the owner.

6. REPLACEMENT HOUSING PAYMENT - HOMEOWNERS

A. If you own and occupy a dwelling to be purchased by the Displacing Agency for at least 180
  days prior to the initiation of negotiations (or otherwise as provided in 25 CCR §6102), you
  may be eligible to receive a payment to assist you in purchasing a comparable replacement
  unit. This payment is not to exceed $22,500, except in the case of Last Resort Housing
  situations, and is intended to cover the following items:

  1.  Purchase Price Differential - An amount which, when added to the amount for
  which the Displacing Agency purchased your property, equals the lesser of the
  actual cost of your replacement dwelling or the amount determined by the
  Displacing Agency as necessary to purchase a comparable replacement dwelling.
  Your relocation agent will explain both methods to you.
  2.  Mortgage Interest Differential - The amount which covers the increased
  interest costs, if any, required to finance a replacement dwelling. Your relocation
  agent will explain limiting conditions.
  3.  Incidental Expenses - Those one time incidental costs related to purchasing a
  replacement unit, such as escrow fees, recording fees, and credit report fees.
  Recurring expenses such as prepaid taxes and insurance premiums are not
  compensable.

B.  Rental Assistance Option - If you are an owner-occupant and choose to rent rather
  than purchase a replacement dwelling, then in lieu of items 1-3 above, you may be eligible
  for a rental assistance payment, not to exceed $5,250 except in the case of Last Resort
  Housing situations, based on the difference between an economic rent of the dwelling you
  occupy and the rent you must pay for a comparable replacement dwelling over a 42-
  month period pursuant to 25 CCR §6112(c)(5)(C).

  If you receive a rental assistance payment, as described above, and later decide to
  purchase a replacement dwelling, you may apply for a payment equal to the amount you
  would have received if you had initially purchased a comparable replacement dwelling,
  less the amount you have already received as a rental assistance payment.

7. SPACE RENT DIFFERENTIAL PAYMENT - HOMEOWNERS

If you own a dwelling to be purchased by the Displacing Agency for at least 180 days prior to
the initiation of negotiations and will be purchasing a comparable replacement unit in another
mobilehome park, you may be eligible to receive a payment to assist you in renting a comparable

If you rent your Park coach, you may be eligible for a payment to assist you in renting or
purchasing a comparable replacement dwelling. In order to qualify, you must either be a tenant

A. Rental Assistance. If you qualify, and wish to rent your replacement dwelling, your

  purchase of a comparable replacement dwelling where such purchase is financed, plus
  expenses incident to the purchase of a replacement dwelling. Your relocation agent will clarify
  procedures necessary to apply for this payment.

Where a tenant is sharing a dwelling with an owner-occupant and paying the owner-occupant
rent for the privilege, the tenant shall not be entitled to more than one-half of the rental assistance
otherwise payable.

9. QUALIFICATION FOR, AND FILING OF, RELOCATION CLAIMS

To qualify for a Replacement Housing Payment, you must rent or purchase and occupy a
comparable replacement unit within one year from the following:

  •  For a tenant, the date you move from the displacement dwelling.
  •  For an owner-occupant, the latter of:
  a. The date you receive final payment for the displacement dwelling, or, in the case

  in court,: or
  b. The date you move from the displacement dwelling.

All claims for relocation benefits must be filed with the Displacing Agency within eighteen (18)
months from the date on which you receive final payment for your property, or the date on
which you move, whichever is later.

10. LAST RESORT HOUSING ASSISTANCE

If comparable replacement dwellings are not available when you are required to move, or are not
available within the monetary limits described above, the Displacing Agency will provide Last
Resort Housing assistance to enable you to rent or purchase a replacement dwelling on a timely
basis. Last Resort Housing assistance is based on the individual circumstances of the displaced
person, as provided in the approved Relocation Impact Report. Your relocation agent will explain
the process for determining whether or not you qualify for Last Resort assistance.

If you are a tenant, and you choose to purchase rather than rent a comparable replacement
dwelling, the entire amount of your rental assistance and Last Resort eligibility must be applied
toward the down-payment and eligible incidental expenses of the home you intend to purchase.

11. EVICTIONS

Any person, who occupies the real property and is not in unlawful occupancy, is presumed to be
entitled to relocation benefits. Except for the causes of eviction set forth below, no person lawfully
occupying property to be developed by the Agency will be required to move without having been
provided with at least 180 days written notice from the Agency. Pursuant to 25 CCR §6058, to
the extent applicable, eviction will be undertaken only in the event of one or more of the following
reasons:

•  Failure to pay rent; except in those cases where the failure to pay is due to the lessor's failure
  to keep the premises in habitable condition, is the result of harassment or retaliatory action
  or is the result of discontinuation or substantial interruption of services;
•  Performance of dangerous illegal act in the unit;
•  Material breach of the rental agreement and failure to correct breach within the legally
  prescribed notice period;
•  Maintenance of a nuisance and failure to abate within a reasonable time following notice;
•  Refusal to accept one of a reasonable number of offers of replacement dwellings; or
•  The eviction is required by State or local law and cannot be prevented by reasonable efforts
  on the part of the public entity.

The Displacing Agency reserves all rights and remedies available to it pursuant to California Civil
Code Section 798.56.

12. TERMINATION OF RELOCATION ASSISTANCE

The Displacing Agency’s relocation obligations will cease under the circumstances set forth in 25
CCR Section 6056.

  Definition of Chattel:

  Chattel refers to tangible, movable personal property that is not classified as real estate and is not permanently affixed to

  livestock, and personal belongings. In modern usage, chattel typically denotes items of personal property that are movable

  (Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School - https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/fee_simple)

  Definition of "Extraordinary Assumption":

  According to the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP), an extraordinary assumption is: “An
  assumption, directly related to a specific assignment, as of the effective date of the appraisal results, which, if found to be
  false, could alter the appraiser’s opinions or conclusions.”

  Extraordinary assumptions are used when the appraiser must presume as fact otherwise uncertain information about:
  - Physical, legal, or economic characteristics of the subject property
  - Conditions external to the subject property, such as market trends or environmental factors
  - The integrity or reliability of data used in the analysis
  The use of an extraordinary assumption may have a direct impact on the final value conclusion. If the assumption is later
  found to be false, the credibility of the appraisal results may be affected. The use of an Extraordinary Assumption might
  have affected the assignment results.

  Definition of "Hypothetical Condition":

  According to the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP), a Hypothetical Condition is:

  "that which is contrary to what exists but is supposed for the purpose of analysis."

  Explanation:

  In appraising, a hypothetical condition is used when an appraiser needs to analyze or value a property as if a certain
  situation existed, even though it doesn't currently exist. The appraiser must clearly state the hypothetical condition and
  explain the impact it has on the valuation.

  For example, an appraiser might use a hypothetical condition to value a vacant lot as if the proposed structure had already
  been built, or to value a burned-out building as if it were fully restored.

  Definition of Market Value:

  The most probable price which a property should bring in a competitive and open market under all conditions requisite to a
  fair sale, the buyer and seller, each acting prudently, knowledgeably and assuming the price is not affected by undue
  stimulus. Implicit in this definition is the consummation of a sale as of a specified date and the passing of title from seller to
  buyer under conditions whereby: (1) buyer and seller are typically motivated; (2) both parties are well informed or well
  advised, and each acting in what he or she considers his or her own best interest; (3) a reasonable time is allowed for
  exposure in the open market; (4) payment is made in terms of cash in U. S. dollars or in terms of financial arrangements
  comparable thereto; and (5) the price represents the normal consideration for the property sold unaffected by special or
  creative financing or sales concessions* granted by anyone associated with the sale.

  *Adjustments to the comparables must be made for special or creative financing or sales concessions. No adjustments are
  necessary for those costs which are normally paid by sellers as a result of tradition or law in a market area; these costs are
  readily identifiable since the seller pays these costs in virtually all sales transactions. Special or creative financing
  adjustments can be made to the comparable property by comparisons to financing terms offered by a third-party
  institutional lender that is not already involved in the property or transaction. Any adjustment should not be calculated on a
  mechanical dollar for dollar cost of the financing or concession but the dollar amount of any adjustment should
  approximate the market’s reaction to the financing or concessions based on the appraiser’s judgment.

  Data Sources for non-typical Manufactured Housing and RV Comparables:

  For appraising manufactured housing (often referred to as mobile homes or trailers) and Recreational Vehicles (RVs),
  standard Multiple Listing Service (MLS) or county tax records often do not provide sufficient sales data because these
  items are frequently titled as personal property (chattel) rather than real property.

  The most reliable sources for finding sales data and valuation assistance for comparison are specialized, industry-specific
  data providers:

  1. Manufactured Housing (Mobile/Trailer Homes)

  This data is crucial when appraising manufactured homes that are considered personal property (e.g., they are not
  permanently affixed to the land, or the land is leased).

  NADA Manufactured Housing Appraisal Guide (J.D. Power Valuation):

  - Description: This is the industry-standard guide for establishing the retail, wholesale, and loan values of manufactured
  homes. It is widely used by lenders and appraisers for personal property valuations.

  - What you find: Model numbers, dimensions, original year of manufacture, optional features, and adjustments for
  condition and location.

  - Use Case: Provides a credible, authoritative source for determining the replacement or benchmark value of the unit
  itself.

  State-Specific Registration/Title Records:

  - Description: In some states, the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) or equivalent agency registers manufactured
  homes and records transfers of ownership, similar to cars.

  - What you find: Official sale price and date of transfer, especially for private transactions not tracked by NADA.

  Dealer Networks and Market Surveys:

  - Description: Sometimes, contacting local dealers or running a localized market survey is necessary to confirm true
  market trends and sales concessions.

  2. Recreational Vehicles (RVs)

  RVs are almost universally considered personal property, and their valuation is akin to vehicle appraisal.

  NADA RV Appraisal Guide (J.D. Power Valuation):

  - Description: The authoritative source for valuing all classes of RVs (Class A, B, C motorhomes, travel trailers, fifth
  wheels, etc.).

  - What you find: Clean retail value, low retail value, wholesale figures, and adjustments based on mileage, condition, and
  optional equipment.

  - Use Case: Essential for providing grounded comparable sales data and necessary condition adjustments.

  Specialized RV Sales Websites (For Market Insight):

  - Description: Websites like RVTrader, dealerships' online inventory, and private sales listings can provide real-time
  indicators of asking prices and time-on-market, helping to bracket the NADA values.

B. SUMMARY

The 151-space Bell Mobile Home Park (8.56 acres) (“Park”) was privately developed in
1946. Currently, residences occupy only 115 of the 151 Park spaces. BCHA acquired it
in 1995 and refinanced it in 2005 by issuing a $20.8 million bond to cover Park costs and
other expenses. BCHA makes the payments on the bond and pays for the upkeep and
maintenance of the Park from rents collected, the latter of which are insufficient to cover
the increasing costs. For several years BCHA has been suffering an increasing structural
deficit, requiring BCHA to utilize reserve funds and at times has borrowed from the City
of Bell’s General Fund to compensate for the deficit.

While this report will focus on Bell Mobile Home Park, both Bell Mobile and Florence
Village Mobile Home parks are pledged as security for the bonds associated with the
purchase of the parks.

  2.  RIR Mitigation Recommendations
This RIR is required by the State of California Government Code and the MRL. The RIR’s
purpose is to report on the impact of a proposed Park closure or conversion upon the
residents of the Park. Approval of the RIR does not mean the Park will close or be
subject to conversion. The Board must make that determination in a separate action.

In order to prepare this Report, OPC reviewed resident data provided by the owners and
conducted a comprehensive study of mobile home park resources and other replacement
housing resources. Consistent with the MRL and the Government Code, this RIR
presents recommendations concerning the mitigation of relocation impacts associated
with the closure of the Park if occurs.

The RIR’s proposed mitigation proposed in the RIR address all applicable legal
requirements. There are three sets of mitigation measures: One set applies to those
situations where it is feasible to relocate the mobile home; another set applies when it is
not feasible to relocate the mobile home; and a third applies to non-owner tenants of the
mobile home.

  a.  Home Relocation

When it is feasible to relocate the mobile home, the proposed mitigation measures would
include the following:

  without limitation, to disassemble, transport, reassemble, and level the mobile
  home and all legal accessory structures (awnings, skirting, porches, storage
  structures, etc.) to another mobile home park within 50 miles of the Park.

  2.  Full replacement cost of any items damaged during the move, substantiated
  by receipts or appraisals from a licensed appraiser.

  3.  Transportation of the home by a licensed, bonded, and insured mover, who
  will disconnect and reconnect all utilities and obtain all required permits.

  4.  Compensation to install improvements, if required at the new park, such as
  new steel supporting piers, skirting, and/or landscaping.

  5.  Payment of temporary lodging and food expenses or daily living expenses,
  if the mobile home relocation results in the homeowner being displaced over
  one or more days, limited to current housing and per diem rates for Los Angeles

BCHA Options and Staff Recommendations

Since 2013 , BCHA has been aware that it was operating very close to structural deficits
based on expenses vs. revenues; that is compounded by significant maintenance and
infrastructure repairs; continuing decline in revenues and increasing operational costs
would create an unbalanced operating budget and require the use of reserve funds and/or
the use of City’s General Fund. Now more than 13 years later, BCHA has consistently
operated with a structural deficit utilizing reserves and any one-time revenue to cover
deficits; however, that budget practice has led to fiscal instability and insolvency that will
negatively impact the City’s General Fund. Based on these facts, staff believe there are
only two via options forthe Board to consider:

1.  No Action Alternative: This is essentially the path BCHA operated under since
  2013, which is no longer fiscally sustainable. It is very difficult for a public agency
  to manage a mobile home park and increase revenues to maintain infrastructure
  and cover the costs of deferred maintenance. This option would create a significant
  exposure to the City’s General Fund immediately with the liabilities and costs
  associated with this non-action.
2.  Sell/Closure of the Parks Subject to Providing Benefits in the RIR: Under this
  option BCHA would evaluate a Buyer that would be able to propose a change in
  use but would be required to provide all the relocation mitigation measures
  provided in the RIR in the event of closure of the Park. Also, if the parks are sold,
  the City’s priority is to facilitate the production of new affordable housing for
  families and senior citizens. If the closure did not occur within five (5) years, a new
  RIR would be required to be approved by the City. Also, ta6 months’ notice to
  residents is required for an intended closure of the Park.

Nothwithstanding the above discussion, the purpose of this discussion is to recommend
the Board review and approval of the RIR. Staff is not recommending an immediate
closure of the park, only approval of the RIR.

Conclusion

For the reasons stated above, staff recommend that the Mayor and City Council approve
the RIR for Gage Mobile Home Park. This approval will guarantee that residents of Gage
Mobile Home Park will receive their financial assistance if the park is sold or closed in the
future.
